findings.title: Gateway local classification misses common relay markers
findings.scenario: authorizeBridge treats a request as workstation (local) when Host is loopback and the TCP peer is loopback, unless a relay marker is present. The marker check is the PROXY_HEADERS list plus the regex /^(x-forwarded-|x-original-|cf-)/ plus front-end-https and x-url-scheme. Headers from other common relays are not covered. Probed: Host localhost, peer 127.0.0.1, and a single header of x-rewrite-url, tailscale-user-login, x-envoy-external-address, fastly-client-ip or x-vercel-forwarded-for each return {local:true,token:null}, so a relayed remote request would receive the workstation bearer token (host-bridge.server.ts:53-58 hands the workstation token to the Host for local). Precondition: a relay on this machine that rewrites Host to a loopback name, forwards from a loopback peer, and adds none of the covered markers. The configured cloudflared connector adds cf-* headers and is refused, so this is not reachable through the stated tunnel.
findings.evidence: Probe in a temp folder importing host-bridge.server.ts by file URL with BUNNY_REMOTE_ORIGIN set. Cases with cf-ray, x-forwarded-proto, Forwarded, single bunny_device cookie, and Bunny_Device cookie were refused as intended. Cases with the five headers above returned local:true. Multi-cookie appended headers were refused, since undici joins cookie values with '; ' so the cookie check still sees them.
findings.recommendation: Make local access an allow-list instead of a deny-list: require that no header outside a small benign set is present (or at least refuse any header whose name is not one a direct browser request sends). Alternatively document that loopback-Host relays are unsupported and keep the current check.

findings.title: Local/remote split rests on relay headers for header-less loopback forwarders (residual design assumption)
findings.scenario: If an operator exposes the Host through a raw TCP forwarder (for example ssh -R or a plain port forward) that does not add any header, a remote client sending Host: localhost with no cookie is classified local and receives the workstation token; the bunny_device cookie check only catches clients that carry the device cookie. This is inherent to trusting the loopback peer and is not changed by round 3. It is listed so the owner knows the transport trust rests on the connector adding headers.
findings.evidence: Probe: new Request('http://localhost:8080/c', {headers: {}}) with peer 127.0.0.1 returns {local:true,token:null}. The same request with cookie bunny_device=abc is refused (host-bridge.server.ts:42).
findings.recommendation: Document that only header-adding connectors (cloudflared) are supported for remote access, or add a per-install secret header that the connector must inject and the gateway verifies for remote and refuses to treat as local.

result.reasoning: Confirmed by reading src/lib/orch/host-bridge.server.ts (no probe run; no repo files touched). Line 38 classifies a request as relayed only if its header name is in PROXY_HEADERS (cf-connecting-ip, cf-ray, x-forwarded-for, x-real-ip, forwarded, via, cdn-loop, true-client-ip, x-client-ip), matches /^(x-forwarded-|x-original-|cf-)/, or is front-end-https or x-url-scheme. The headers named in the finding (x-rewrite-url, tailscale-user-login, x-envoy-external-address, fastly-client-ip, x-vercel-forwarded-for) match none of these, so a request with Host localhost (or 127.0.0.1, or [::1]) and a loopback TCP peer reaches line 43 and returns {local:true, token:null}. The workstation token is then attached at line 92 (hostCall). The precondition is real but narrow: a relay on this machine must be reachable from outside, rewrite Host to a loopback name, and add none of the covered markers. A default nginx proxy_pass to 127.0.0.1 with no X-Forwarded-For is one plausible example, so this is a genuine deny-list gap, not a refutable non-issue. It is not reachable through the configured cloudflared tunnel, which always adds cf-* headers and is refused at line 39. Severity stays LOW as hardening: the peer-loopback requirement and the header refusals still hold for the stated deployment. The recommendation to move to an allow-list or to document loopback-Host relays as unsupported is reasonable.

The finding is real and reproduced; I am not refuting it, but I rate it higher than LOW because the impact is full workstation authority, not a read leak.

Code path: src/lib/orch/host-bridge.server.ts:23-49. A request is local when Host is loopback and the TCP peer is loopback (line 28). The only relay defences are the PROXY_HEADERS list, the regex /^(x-forwarded-|x-original-|cf-)/, front-end-https and x-url-scheme (lines 37-39), plus the bunny_device cookie check (line 42). Any relay that rewrites or preserves a loopback Host and adds none of those headers is classified local. hostCall (line 92) then sends the workstation bearer token to the Host.

Probe (temp folder, deleted afterwards; repo untouched): Host localhost or 127.0.0.1, peer 127.0.0.1, no markers, GET => {local:true, token:null}. Same with x-rewrite-url => local:true. A POST with an Origin of the remote origin throws "Origin mismatch." (line 33). A POST with no Origin, which is what any non-browser client sends, returns local:true. A cf-ray header is refused, so the configured cloudflared tunnel is safe. A non-loopback peer is refused.

Why MEDIUM rather than LOW: the Origin check only stops browser-originated cross-origin requests. A non-browser client reaching such a relay can omit Origin and send POST commands, which hostCall forwards with the workstation token. Under that precondition the remote caller acts as the workstation and can approve the very operations the device policy forbids. The precondition is a relay the operator adds that is not the configured tunnel. A default nginx proxy_pass to 127.0.0.1 with no proxy_set_header meets it: Host becomes the loopback upstream and no forwarding headers are added. The code comment on line 8 shows the designers expected proxies and chose a deny-list, so this is a fail-open gap in defence in depth rather than a bypass of the stated tunnel path. The recommended allow-list or a documented unsupported-relay rule is appropriate.

findings.title: Trusted-desktop grant binds the project state at mint, not at ask: a device-approved write between the desktop ask and allow_once is executed under the grant
findings.scenario: A Mission has two independent steps: step 1 is filesystem.write helper.mjs (ask_every_time, so a device can answer it) and step 2 is terminal.exec node probe.mjs, where probe.mjs imports ./helper.mjs. Both asks are pending. The paired device answers the write allow_once, which writes device-modified content to helper.mjs. The workstation then answers the terminal ask allow_once. The ask-time reason lists no changed files, because remoteChanges() runs at ask time (manager.server.ts ~3261) and the write happened after the ask. mintDesktopGrant() (line 2215, called from respond() at 3456) snapshots store.mutationSequence() at mint time, and desktopBinding (~3276-3281) does not carry the ask-time sequence or the file identities. The grant therefore validates against the post-write state and the workstation-approved command runs the device-written module. The accepted-limitation mitigation ('the prompt lists them') covers only writes made before the ask.
findings.evidence: Probe (node --experimental-strip-types, repo modules imported by file URL, temp dir deleted): runAskBefore.reason = 'Approval required on Windows Host: a paired device cannot authorize command or code execution. terminal.exec runs a program.' with no helper.mjs mention; helperAfterDeviceWrite = "export const v = 'device-modified';" (device answer accepted, runAskStillOpen = true); after workstation allow_once, grantMinted = true and ranTxt = "device-modified". Relevant code: src/lib/bunny-missions/store.server.ts:149-153 (mutationSequence), manager.server.ts:2131-2143 (desktopContext reads the sequence at call time), manager.server.ts:2215-2227 (mint), manager.server.ts:3261 (remoteChanges at ask time), manager.server.ts:3276-3281 (desktopBinding lacks sequence).
findings.recommendation: Capture mutationSequence (and the file identities for named scripts and cwd-resolved files) in desktopBinding when the ask is raised, and refuse the mint when either differs from the current value. Alternatively, recompute remoteChanges at mint and refuse if it is non-empty. Add a regression test equal to the probe above: a device write between ask and allow_once must void the grant or re-ask.

findings.title: terminal.exec content binding ignores params.cwd: the executed script in the working subfolder is not hashed, so editing it leaves the approved operation identical
findings.scenario: A terminal.exec step with params {command:'node', args:['probe.mjs'], cwd:'sub'} is approved. fileIdentities() resolves each named argument against the Mission cwd (request.cwd), not against the folder the process actually starts in. The terminal adapter runs in cwdOf(params) (local.server.ts:27-29, launch at :153), i.e. root/sub, so it executes root/sub/probe.mjs. That file is never hashed, and the operation digest contains only the cwd string. Any edit to root/sub/probe.mjs between ask and mint is invisible to the grant check. Edits after mint are caught by the mutation sequence, so the window is the ask-to-mint interval (same root cause as the HIGH finding).
findings.evidence: Probe: capabilityOperation('terminal.exec', {command:'node',args:['probe.mjs'],cwd:'sub'}, root, null) yields files = {} when root/sub/probe.mjs exists, and JSON.stringify of the operation is identical after overwriting sub/probe.mjs with different content (sameOperationAfterEdit = true). Code: authorization.server.ts:298-313 (fileIdentities resolves against cwd argument), :315-317 (capabilityOperation passes request.cwd), capabilities/local.server.ts:27-29 and :153-160 (process runs in params.cwd). The policy requires content hashes of named script files.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the terminal execution folder with the same rule the adapter uses (params.cwd resolved within the request roots) before hashing, and hash the resolved script arguments relative to that folder. Include the resolved execution folder in DesktopOperation. Add a test that editing a script named under a cwd subfolder changes the operation.

findings.title: Binding completeness note: the session operation does not cover the composed prompt, and the plan reference omits step objectives
findings.scenario: sessionOperation() binds provider, model, effort, access, cwd and session authority. The shell-capable session's prompt is built from the step objective plus dependency result summaries (up to 1200 characters each) and memory facts (context.ts:10-24; manager.server.ts:1273-1280). Those summaries come from earlier steps, which may be device-approved tool-free or read-only sessions. agenticPlanReference() (manager.server.ts, definition near the Agentic plan helpers) hashes only id, executor, scope, verification, requiredCapabilities and crossApp data, so step objective and role are not bound. Replan and envelope revocation already void grants, so this is not exploitable through the paths I checked; it is a gap in the binding the owner asked for.
findings.evidence: Code reading only; not probed. Relevant lines: authorization.server.ts:294-296, context.ts:20-24, manager.server.ts:1273-1280, and the agenticPlanReference body.
findings.recommendation: Consider adding a digest of the composed prompt (or of the objective and dependency summaries) to sessionOperation, or state explicitly that the desktop prompt is not bound.

result.reasoning:
Not refuted. I re-read the code paths; no probe was run and no repo file was touched or tested.

Confirmed in code:
- manager.server.ts:3266-3268: remoteChanges(mission) runs once at ask time and only those paths are written into the reason text.
- manager.server.ts:3283-3286: desktopBinding captures only taskId, authorizationId and planReference. It has no mutationSequence and no file identities.
- manager.server.ts:2146-2158 (desktopContext) and 2220-2228 (mintDesktopGrant): mutationSequence is read at mint time, so a write that lands between ask and allow_once is absorbed into the grant. The binding comparison at 2225 does not catch it.
- authorization.server.ts:267: the use-time check compares the grant's sequence with the current one. Because the grant was minted after the write, it passes.
- Imported modules are not covered by the ask-time operation. capabilityOperation (authorization.server.ts:237-238) hashes only the command params, plus fileIdentities for named script and --opt=file arguments. A helper module imported by probe.mjs is not hashed, so only mutationSequence could bind it.

Reachability: tickOnce (manager.server.ts ~910-916) admits every ready step up to maxConcurrentAgents, whose default is 3 (store.server.ts:13). So two steps with no dependsOn edge can both be pending: a filesystem.write ask on helper.mjs and a terminal.exec ask on probe.mjs. A device answer to the write executes during the terminal ask, and remoteChanges has already been computed. The planner-produced DAG decides whether this happens, but it is a normal concurrent case.

Impact: the accepted-limitation text says device-written code run by a desktop-approved command is acceptable because "the prompt lists them". That mitigation fails for writes that occur after the ask, so the workstation approves "node probe.mjs" without being told helper.mjs changed. This is an informed-consent failure in an owner-accepted design, not a fully new bypass, so I rate it HIGH as claimed, though MEDIUM would be defensible. The fix in the recommendation (bind the sequence or file identities at ask time, or recompute remoteChanges at mint) is sound.

Not refuted. I reproduced the finding with a throwaway probe in a mkdtemp folder under the OS temp dir (deleted afterwards). Setup: a Mission with two parallel, dependency-free steps (filesystem.write helper.mjs under an ask_every_time grant, and terminal.exec node probe.mjs, where probe.mjs imports ./helper.mjs), approved by a paired device with start=true. Both asks were open. The terminal ask reason at ask time was "Approval required on Windows Host: a paired device cannot authorize command or code execution. terminal.exec runs a program." with no file list. The device answered the write allow_once (accepted, desktopRequired null). The write applied and the terminal ask stayed open. Afterwards remoteChanges() reports helper.mjs, but the stored terminal reason was not updated. The workstation allow_once then minted a grant (grantMinted=true) and the run completed with ran.txt = "device-modified". So the device-written module executed under a workstation approval whose prompt did not list it. Code references: manager.server.ts mintDesktopGrant (~2215) and desktopContext (~2131) read store.mutationSequence() at mint/ask time respectively; the desktopBinding built at ~3276-3281 carries taskId/authorizationId/planReference only, not the sequence or file identities; remoteChanges is evaluated once at ask time (~3261). The accepted limitation the owner recorded depends on the prompt listing device-changed files; that mitigation does not cover writes made after the ask and before the answer, so the stated justification does not hold for this path. Severity kept at HIGH since the device causes device-authored code to run under a workstation approval that did not disclose it. The fix suggested by the finding (bind the mutation sequence or file identities at ask time and refuse mint on mismatch, plus a regression test) is sound. Repo files were not modified; no repo tests were run.

findings.title: Device mission.start and agent.resume gates skip workstation-held EXECUTE computer capabilities
findings.scenario: A workstation-approved plan contains a crossApp computer.open_app step with app 'terminal' (APPS.terminal = wt.exe, computer.server.ts:13, 459-462, 533). scopeFor adds EXECUTE to riskClasses for crossApp computer steps (authorization.server.ts:67), so decide() allows the step under the workstation envelope with no desktop approval. A paired device calling mission.start (commands.server.ts:60) gets deviceStartRefusal() = null, because its shell check only tests terminal.* and git commit/merge/worktree (manager.server.ts:2103-2104). The mission then launches Windows Terminal on the workstation. The same holds for computer.invoke_control or computer.focus_window on any window (not only Calculator). For agent.resume, deviceResumeRefusal() (manager.server.ts:2114-2115, called from agent-runtime.server.ts:217) checks only terminal.exec and git mutations, so a workstation-consented Agent whose permitted_capabilities include computer.open_app or computer.invoke_control resumes on device request. The policy names arbitrary executable launches through indirect capabilities and says devices never decide when workstation-held code execution begins. The round-1 fix applied that rule to terminal and Git, but not to these EXECUTE capabilities. The paired-device execution ceiling (remoteExecutionRefusal, authorization.server.ts:205) refuses these exact operations for remote envelopes, so the workstation-envelope start path is inconsistent with it. Not covered by remote-authority.test.ts (F01-R5 and F01-R11 cover only terminal.exec and sessions).
findings.evidence: Probe (throwaway, mkdtemp under /tmp, deleted): workstation envelope with capabilities [computer.open_app], riskClasses [EXECUTE], computer.enabled true, providers.execution false, terminal disabled, git actions empty -> MissionManager.prototype.deviceStartRefusal.call(...) = null. decide(open_app, {app:'terminal'}, workstation envelope) = allow ('Inside mission authorization'). Agent permitted_capabilities [computer.open_app, computer.invoke_control] -> deviceResumeRefusal = null. Same envelope with grantedBy device -> remoteExecutionRefusal(open_app terminal) = 'Approval required on Windows Host ... not an exact reviewed Calculator operation'. Invoke_control on 'Windows Terminal' with workstation envelope -> allow.
findings.recommendation: In deviceStartRefusal and deviceResumeRefusal, refuse any workstation envelope or consent whose capabilities include an EXECUTE-risk action that is not an exact reviewed Calculator operation, using the same remoteExecutionRefusal rule with the manifest risk (or the envelope riskClasses). Add regression tests in remote-authority.test.ts for computer.open_app(terminal) and computer.invoke_control on a non-Calculator window, covering mission.start and agent.resume.

findings.title: Relaunch gate ignores envelope expiry (pre-existing, LOW)
findings.scenario: missionScopeCheck (manager.server.ts:94-112) rejects a missing or revoked envelope but never tests expiresAt. providerScopeViolation (authorization.server.ts:432-460) has no expiry test either. The gate runs for every provider session start, including startSession relaunches for retry-same, reroute, escalate-effort and larger-context (bunny-host/manager.server.ts:1286-1288, 1338, 1543-1587). Expiry is checked only by taskViolation (authorization.server.ts:448, used on the step-launch and approveDelegated path) and by deviceRequestRefusal (manager.server.ts:2012). So an envelope past expiresAt can still relaunch a session through automatic retry or reroute. For a device-approved remote envelope this means tool-free Ollama inference continues after the approved window. Workstation envelopes are affected the same way for shell sessions, but no device action triggers those. The gap predates the T9R diff, and the diff's rewrite of this closure did not add the check. Code-read only; not probed, because the closure needs a full MissionManager.
findings.evidence: manager.server.ts:94-112 (no expiresAt test); authorization.server.ts:448 (taskViolation expiry check); manager.server.ts:2012 (device answer expiry check); bunny-host/manager.server.ts:1286-1288 (relaunch gate).
findings.recommendation: Add an expiresAt <= now refusal to missionScopeCheck (both check and launch phases), so every session start, relaunch included, honors the envelope window. Add a test that a relaunch after expiry is refused.

findings.title: Device approval of Claude read-only sessions is refused, narrower than owner policy (fail-closed)
findings.scenario: The owner policy says devices may approve Claude read-only sessions. deviceMayLaunch admits only Ollama (TOOL_FREE_PROVIDERS = {ollama}), and deviceRequestRefusal sends every provider.execute ask through it (manager.server.ts ~2012-2016). A device therefore cannot answer a claude-read provider.execute request even when policy allows it. Remote envelopes do allow claude read by their own ceiling (remoteSessionViolation returns null for read_tools), so the two paths disagree. This is fail-closed and not a security defect.
findings.evidence: Probe: deviceMayLaunch({provider:'claude', model:'sonnet'}, []) = false; deviceMayLaunch({provider:'ollama', model:'llama3'}, []) = true.
findings.recommendation: Decide whether device approval of claude read-only sessions should be enabled, per policy. If so, extend deviceRequestRefusal to accept claude with access read and no shell, and add a test.

findings.title: Remote-approved source writes are not surfaced to later workstation-approved executions
findings.scenario: Workstation creates Mission M1 with a filesystem.write of probe.mjs and a paired device approves it; the bounded write is allowed remotely with no prompt. Later the workstation creates Mission M2 (workstation envelope) running terminal.exec node probe.mjs and approves it. M2 runs with no ask and no notice, executing the file the device-approved write changed. remoteChanges(M2) is empty because it is scoped to one Mission (store.runs filtered by missionId), and the listing at manager.server.ts:3272 only runs when desktop.desktopRequired is set, which never happens for a workstation envelope. The owner's accepted limitation for source files written under paired-device authority relies on the prompt listing those files; that mitigation does not cover this cross-Mission or workstation-envelope path.
findings.evidence: Probe (throwaway, mkdtemp, deleted): M1 authority kind=remote, actor device:t9r-f01-phone; M1 remoteChanges=["probe.mjs"]; M2 state=completed, M2 requests=[], M2 remoteChanges=[], M2 ranChangedFile=true (cross-ran.txt written by the remote-approved content); M2 authority kind=workstation; M2 run status=succeeded, decisionReason 'Inside mission authorization ...'.
findings.recommendation: Make the changed-file disclosure project-scoped: list every paired-device-authorized mutation in the folder since the last workstation review, and show it on any later workstation approval that can execute code there (or refuse terminal/session runs over such files until the workstation reviews them). Alternatively void workstation terminal grants when a remote mutation lands in their folder. Owner may reasonably classify this as BLOCKER because it lets a device change what a workstation-approved command executes.

findings.title: Device command responses expose trusted-desktop grant, operation and binding records
findings.scenario: MissionManager.view() returns requests with desktopGrant, desktopOperation and desktopBinding unfiltered. mission.approve, mission.respond, mission.start and mission.stop in commands.server.ts (lines 52, 65-79) return that view directly to a paired device. Only mission.get (commands.server.ts:80) and the snapshot path (remoteVerdicts) strip these fields. The remoteVerdicts comment says devices never see grant or exact-operation records, so the stated policy is not met. A device cannot spend or mint a grant from these records, so this is disclosure, not authority.
findings.evidence: Probe through missionCommand as device:t9r-f01-phone: after the workstation allow_once on request 1 (desktopGrant.uses=1) and device deny on request 2, the mission.respond response includes request 1 with keys desktopRequired, desktopOperation, desktopBinding, desktopGrant. desktopOperation exposed cwd, executable file path and SHA-256 file identities; desktopGrant exposed id and uses. mission.get for the same device returned only desktopRequired.
findings.recommendation: Route every device-facing mission response through the same projection as mission.get (deviceMissionData or a shared stripper in view()), and add an assertion for mission.respond/approve/stop responses.

findings.title: Execution-config classifier omits task and hook configs its own comment names
findings.scenario: EXECUTION_CONFIG_FILE covers Git drivers, package scripts and npm/yarn/pnpm/bun config, but not task or hook runners. A paired device can approve a bounded filesystem.write of Taskfile.yml, justfile, lefthook.yml, .pre-commit-config.yaml, conftest.py, pyproject.toml or build.rs, because remoteExecutionRefusal returns null for them. A later workstation-approved command such as task build, just, pytest, or pip install . then executes that content. The comment at lines 122 says the set covers 'tasks' and 'hooks'. This overlaps the accepted limitation for arbitrary source files, but these names are the category the code claims to protect.
findings.evidence: Probe calling remoteExecutionRefusal('filesystem.write', {path}, 'WRITE', proj) returned null for Taskfile.yml, justfile, lefthook.yml, .pre-commit-config.yaml, conftest.py, pyproject.toml, build.rs and vitest.config.ts. The same call refused package.json, .git/hooks/x, .git., and .git /config.
findings.recommendation: Add the task-runner and hook config names (Taskfile.yml/.yaml, justfile, lefthook.yml, .pre-commit-config.yaml, pyproject.toml, setup.py/cfg, conftest.py, build.rs, Rakefile, Gemfile, tox.ini, noxfile.py) or document them as accepted with the same reasoning as source files.

findings.title: Synchronous filesystem probing on the remote gate can stall the Host event loop for seconds
findings.scenario: resolvedNames() calls existsSync and realpathSync.native synchronously on the requested path. Unreachable UNC paths block for seconds. remoteVerdicts (manager.server.ts ~2061) calls deviceRequestRefusal, which calls remoteExecutionRefusal and executionConfigPath, for every unresolved request on every device snapshot. A workstation-authored pending filesystem.write to a UNC path would therefore stall the Host event loop on every device poll. A device cannot choose the path, so reachability is limited to workstation-authored plans.
findings.evidence: Probe: executionConfigPath/touchesGitMetadata on '\\\\server\\share\\x' took 5528 ms synchronously; local, nonexistent and device-name paths took 0-2 ms.
findings.recommendation: Treat UNC and other non-local roots as desktop-required without probing the filesystem, or move the probe off the event loop and cache its verdict per request.

findings.title: Mutation sequence does not count provider-session file writes
findings.scenario: The grant binding claims any project change after approval voids the grant, but mutationSequence() counts only capability_runs rows for filesystem/git/browser/terminal actions. Writes made by a desktop-approved shell provider session do not bump it, and the Mission conflict registry (desktopExecutions) covers capability runs and session tasks but not session file writes. Only named script files are content-hashed. An approved terminal.exec that imports an unnamed module which a concurrent approved session rewrites would not be voided. I did not find a device-reachable path, because remote envelopes cannot start write-capable sessions.
findings.evidence: Code reading only; not probed. SQL at store.server.ts:150 selects action IN (filesystem.write, filesystem.delete, git.*, browser.download, terminal.exec) from capability_runs.
findings.recommendation: Bump the sequence (or record a project-tree digest) when any write-capable provider session starts or finishes, and correct the grant comment.

findings.title: Device single allow_once authorizes writes and reads outside the approved project roots (one-time roots extension)
findings.scenario: A workstation-authored Mission whose plan has a filesystem.write (or filesystem.read) capability step with an absolute path outside envelope.projectRoots. The phone approves the plan (deviceMissionRefusal only checks risk classes). The step asks 'outside the approved write scope'. The phone answers allow_once. decide() returns allow for oneTime at line 346, before scopeViolation at line 359 is reached. capabilityRequest() then extends the one-time roots to dirname(path) (manager.server.ts ~1489-1492), so FilesystemCapability writes the file outside the project, e.g. a Windows Startup folder .cmd (runs at next logon), %USERPROFILE%\.gitconfig, or Host source files. Reads outside the root are exfiltrated the same way. deviceRequestRefusal() (manager.server.ts ~2023-2028) judges only the planned params through remoteExecutionRefusal(), which checks Git/execution-config names, not envelope scope, so the device gate passes. This violates the policy that devices approve only bounded ordinary in-scope writes and never indirect executable launches.
findings.evidence: Throwaway probes in an own mkdtemp folder: (a) decide(filesystem.write, {path:<root>/outside/Startup/x.cmd}, envelope roots=[proj]) without oneTime returns ask 'is outside the approved write scope'; with oneTime:true returns allow. (b) remoteExecutionRefusal('filesystem.write', same params, 'WRITE', proj) returns null. (c) End-to-end through MissionManager/missionCommand with the remote-authority test harness: mission.approve by device:t9r-f01-phone, then mission.respond allow_once by the phone. Result: request resolution allow_once by device:t9r-f01-phone; run filesystem.write succeeded 'Wrote 13 bytes to <outside>\Startup\probe-startup.cmd'; file exists outside the project; mission completed. No existing remote-authority test covers an out-of-scope single answer (grep of remote-authority.test.ts).
findings.recommendation: Refuse device single answers (allow_once) for any ask whose reason is a scope violation, or whose filesystem path lies outside envelope.projectRoots/filesystem.read/write roots. Judge the path against the envelope in deviceRequestRefusal, not only executionConfigPath. Restrict the dirname roots extension in capabilityRequest to workstation answers, or drop it for remote envelopes. Add a regression test for an out-of-root write and an out-of-root read answered by a phone.

findings.title: Expired remote authorization still executes a device one-time answer
findings.scenario: A remote Mission envelope passes expiresAt. A capability ask is already pending. The phone answers allow_once after expiry. respond() performs no envelope expiry check for allow_once, and decide() returns allow for oneTime at line 346, before the expiry check at line 354. The single action then runs with an expired envelope. The round-2 fix refuses expired envelopes only for provider.execute in deviceRequestRefusal (manager.server.ts ~2011-2013).
findings.evidence: Throwaway end-to-end probe: after the ask was created, the envelope was saved with expiresAt = now-1, then mission.respond allow_once by device:t9r-f01-phone. findings.recommendation: Treat an expired or revoked envelope as a deny before the oneTime allowance in decide(). Also refuse device answers on expired envelopes for every action in deviceRequestRefusal, not only provider.execute.

findings.title: mergeTransaction bypasses the remote Git hardening flags (only reachable with a trusted-desktop grant)
findings.scenario: git.merge is refused for remote envelopes at the bus unless a trusted-desktop grant exists. Once granted, GitCapability.execute calls mergeTransaction(branch, cwd, context) (local.server.ts:284), which uses its own runCommand('git', ...) runner (git-merge.server.ts:15) with no --no-textconv, core.hooksPath, core.fsmonitor or diff.external overrides, even when context.remoteAuthority is true. Hooks and merge drivers run under that desktop-approved operation. This is consistent with the policy (desktop approval lifts the ceiling) and is not a remote bypass, since a remote device cannot plant .git hooks or config. It is an inconsistency with the rest of the remote Git path.
findings.evidence: git-merge.server.ts:15 runner; local.server.ts:284 mergeTransaction call without the remote-hardened runner; all GitCapability.git() invocations are hardened when context.remoteAuthority is set (local.server.ts ~207). No other git spawn sites exist outside tests (grep of runCommand/spawn/execFile).
findings.recommendation: Pass a hardened runner to mergeTransaction when context.remoteAuthority is set, so the remote Git flags apply uniformly, even under a desktop grant.

result.reasoning:
Not refuted. The gap is real and reproducible from code reading plus a probe.

Path confirmed:
1. Device gate passes. deviceRequestRefusal (manager.server.ts:2008-2028) returns null for an in-envelope-agnostic WRITE: deviceApprovalRefusal (device-authority.server.ts:102-109) only rejects EXTERNAL_SIDE_EFFECT/DESTRUCTIVE/sensitive/hardApproval, and remoteExecutionRefusal (authorization.server.ts:201-214) only checks Git mutations and executionConfigPath, not envelope scope. Probe: remoteExecutionRefusal("filesystem.write", {path:<outside>/Startup/x.cmd}, "WRITE", proj) returns null.
2. The answer sets step.approvedOnce (manager.server.ts:3565/3591) with no scope check.
3. capabilityRequest (manager.server.ts:1489-1492) extends roots to dirname(path) when approvedOnce matches, and sets oneTimeAction (1502).
4. CapabilityBus passes oneTime to decide (bus.server.ts:159), and decide returns allow at authorization.server.ts:346 before scopeViolation at line 359.
5. The adapter's scopedPath (local.server.ts:57, paths.server.ts:35) uses request.roots (bus.server.ts:303), so the write proceeds.
6. projectResourceCheck / assertResource (project-context.server.ts:37-70, agent-workspace.server.ts:204) only blocks private Host state, sensitive names, links and cross-project paths. It does not check the envelope or project root, so an outside path passes.

Probe (own mkdtemp dir, removed afterwards): decide(filesystem.write, outside path, remote envelope with roots=[proj]) returns ask "is outside the approved write scope" without oneTime, and allow with oneTime:true. remoteExecutionRefusal returns null. No repo files were modified and no repo tests were run.

Severity: I agree with HIGH rather than BLOCKER. The device causes a single-file write to an arbitrary path outside the workstation-approved roots. That is a permission expansion the policy forbids, and a Startup-folder .cmd would become code execution at next logon, so the BLOCKER argument is arguable. Reads outside the roots are also possible, but private Host state (host.sqlite, credentials.json, remote.json) is still blocked by privateHostPath in assertResource. The finding's line numbers are accurate (346, 359, manager 1489-1492).

Confirmed, not refuted. Probe (throwaway folder, since deleted) of remoteExecutionRefusal("filesystem.write", {path}, "WRITE", proj) in /workspace-equivalent temp project: Taskfile.yml, justfile, lefthook.yml, .pre-commit-config.yaml, conftest.py, pyproject.toml, build.rs, tox.ini, noxfile.py, eslint.config.js, vite.config.ts and src/index.ts all return null (allowed remotely). Makefile and package.json return the DESKTOP_REQUIRED refusal ("configures Git, package scripts, hooks or tasks that run commands"). So the classifier is inconsistent: Makefile (a task runner) is refused, justfile and Taskfile.yml (equivalent task runners) are not, and the comment at authorization.server.ts:122 explicitly claims "tasks" and "hooks". EXECUTION_CONFIG_FILE is at line 123 as stated. Why not MEDIUM: the write is an ordinary bounded file write, a later command still needs a workstation allow_once on terminal.exec (remote terminal.exec is refused at line 203), and the desktop prompt lists files changed under paired-device authority (round-2 fix 19). Overlap with the accepted "arbitrary source files" limitation is partial: Taskfile/justfile/lefthook/pre-commit are declarative command configs of the same class the owner deliberately protected (package.json, Makefile), not source files. Stated severity LOW is appropriate. Also noted, unprobed: sitecustomize.py/usercustomize.py are auto-imported by Python for cwd-based runs and are also absent from the list.

Not refuted: the stall is real but is an availability issue with no device-controlled trigger, so LOW is the right severity.

Mechanism confirmed: src/lib/bunny-missions/authorization.server.ts:136 (existsSync loop) and :142 (realpathSync.native) are synchronous, called from resolvedNames, which is reached via executionConfigPath (:150) and touchesGitMetadata (:146). For a filesystem.write/delete with an absolute UNC path, remoteExecutionRefusal (:211) calls executionConfigPath. A probe in a fresh mkdtemp folder (since deleted) timed `executionConfigPath("\\\\nonexistent-host-zz9\\share\\x")` at 2611 ms, versus 0 ms for a local nonexistent path. The finding's 5528 ms figure is an unreachable-host variant of the same thing.

Reachability is narrower than the finding's wording suggests:
- The trigger is the path, not the poll. Probing runs only for unresolved requests, so a stall needs a pending UNC write or delete.
- Devices cannot create Missions or plans: mission.create is not in commands.server.ts REMOTE (:27), and it is refused for non-local access (:30). Devices cannot supply paths to pending requests, so the path is workstation- or model-authored.
- The probe is not device-specific. http.server.ts:338 calls missions.remoteVerdicts for every principal, and only the device projection differs at :364-365. So the workstation's own /state polls trigger it too. The finding's "every device snapshot" claim is therefore slightly inaccurate, though a device poll does amplify it.
- Each remoteVerdicts pass can probe twice per request (allow_once and, if batchOffer, allow_batch; manager.server.ts:2085-2087). Agent pending items are probed again at http.server.ts:~352 through deviceRequestRefusal. Nothing caches the result.
- The line references in the finding are off: remoteVerdicts is at manager.server.ts:2069 and deviceRequestRefusal at :2008. The reported line 136 is correct.

No device-supplied string reaches resolvedNames. The only other probes are in fileIdentities (existsSync/statSync), which runs at grant mint on the workstation path. The finding's recommendation (classify UNC/non-local roots as desktop-required without probing, or cache per request) is sound.

I did not edit the repo, run repo tests, or touch test-results/. The only probe was a throwaway script in a mkdtemp folder, which was removed.

Not refuted. The stall is real and the code path is reachable, though the finding overstates device control.

Confirmed:
- authorization.server.ts:136 is `while (!existsSync(probe))`, and :142 is `realpathSync.native(probe)`. Both are synchronous and were introduced by this change set (absent at 7fbea39).
- Probe (temp dir, since deleted; no repo test run; test-results untouched): executionConfigPath on \\127.0.0.1\nosuchshare\x.txt took 2115 ms. An unresolvable host (nonexistent-host-zz9.invalid) took 112 ms. Local nonexistent and local existing paths took 0 ms. The finding's 5.5 s figure for an unreachable server is plausible but I did not reproduce it exactly.
- Reachability: scopeViolation (authorization.server.ts:283) returns an ask, not a deny, for an out-of-scope write path (line 359). So a filesystem.write to a UNC path becomes a pending request. The remote gate (line 340) then runs remoteExecutionRefusal before the scope check, so the probe runs for remote envelopes too.
- The projection runs on every principal's state: remoteVerdicts is called unconditionally at http.server.ts:338. It is also reached from GET /state (:429) and from command responses (:765). Each pending request costs up to two probes (once and, if batchOffer, the batch variant; manager.server.ts:2085-2087). The workstation's own polling therefore also stalls the Host event loop.

Qualification to the finding: the claim that a device cannot choose the path is weaker than stated. A device creates missions with a free-text objective (commands.server.ts:41-47, device allowed by DEVICE_RIGHTS), and the planner (planMission) decides step paths. I did not verify that the planner can emit a UNC path from a device objective, so reachability through a device is plausible but unproven. Workstation-authored or model-generated plans are a confirmed route.

Additional side effect, not probed: the probe performs DNS and SMB network I/O to an arbitrary host named in a path. Whether this sends Windows credentials to that host was not verified, so I do not claim it.

Severity stays LOW: availability only, no authority escalation, no execution. The recommended fix is sound: have remoteExecutionRefusal return DESKTOP_REQUIRED for any UNC or device-namespace path (\\..., \\?\..., \\.\...) before calling executionConfigPath, so no probe runs. Fail-closed is preserved, since a UNC alias to a local .git (for example \\localhost\C$) is refused rather than probed.

Not refuted. The finding reproduces end to end through the real MissionManager/CapabilityBus/missionCommand boundary, using the remote-authority harness with a phone actor (device:t9r-f01-phone).

Probe results (throwaway mkdtemp folder under the OS temp dir, now deleted):
- WRITE: a workstation-authored mission with filesystem.write to <tmp>/outside/Startup/probe-startup.cmd. The phone approved the mission, and the Host asked "...is outside the approved write scope." with desktopRequired null. The phone's mission.respond allow_once was accepted. The mission completed and the file exists outside the project root.
- READ: filesystem.read of <tmp>/outside/secret.txt. Same flow, the ask was "outside the approved read scope", allow_once was accepted, and the step completed with "Read 13 bytes from ...". I did not verify that the file content reaches the device through mission output.

Code path: authorization.server.ts:346 (`if (context.oneTime) return allow(...)`) runs before scopeViolation at :359. manager.server.ts:1489-1492 extends roots with dirname(path) for a one-time answer. deviceRequestRefusal (manager.server.ts:2008-2024) calls remoteExecutionRefusal, which never checks the envelope roots.

Correction to the finding: its ".gitconfig" example is wrong. remoteExecutionRefusal returns DESKTOP_REQUIRED for ~/.gitconfig (executionConfigPath matches the .gitconfig leaf), so that vector is blocked. The working vector is an ordinary-named script outside the root, such as a .cmd or .ps1 in the Windows Startup folder. executionConfigPath returns false and remoteExecutionRefusal returns null for both. That file runs at the next logon, so a device-authorized write causes code execution, which the policy forbids. I rate it BLOCKER for that reason; the finding's HIGH is defensible if the owner reads deferred execution as narrower.

Nothing in the existing remote-authority tests covers out-of-scope single answers. The workstation's own allow_once extending roots is by design. The defect is that a device may give that answer. Recommended fix: refuse device allow_once for scope-violation asks (or any path outside envelope roots), and add regression tests for an out-of-root write and read answered by a phone. No repo files were edited, and no repo tests were run.</reasoning>

Not refuted. The finding reproduces, and the code matches the claim.

Code paths:
- authorization.server.ts:345-346: the revoked check and then `if (context.oneTime) return allow(...)`. There is no expiry check before the oneTime allow.
- authorization.server.ts:353-354: `envelope.revokedAt` and `envelope.expiresAt <= now` are checked only after the oneTime return, so an expired one-time answer is allowed.
- capabilities/bus.server.ts:159: oneTime is set from `request.oneTime || oneTimeAction === action`, so a single phone answer reaches the allow at line 346 with an expired envelope.
- manager.server.ts:3422-3520 (respond): it checks only request resolution, step state and device refusal. It has no envelope expiry check for allow_once.
- manager.server.ts:2011-2015 (deviceRequestRefusal): the expiry refusal exists only inside the `provider.execute` branch. For other actions, a device answer is refused only for desktopRequired asks, owner-set deviceApprovalRefusal, and remoteExecutionRefusal. A bounded filesystem.write passes all three.

Probe (throwaway, mkdtemp under the OS temp dir, deleted afterwards; no repo files touched, no repo tests run):
- Phone (device:probe-phone) created a capability mission with one filesystem.write step and approved it with start:false.
- The envelope was saved with expiresAt = now-1000 ms, then the mission was started.
- The Host raised pending ask filesystem.write, reason "The mission authorization expired.", with desktopRequired undefined.
- mission.respond allow_once by the phone returned ok. The mission reached state "completed" and late.txt was written with "after expiry".

The Host's own invariant contradicts this. The comment at manager.server.ts:2012 says "a device never extends an expired or revoked envelope", and remote-authority.test.ts:798 asserts "a phone cannot extend an expired envelope". That assertion passes only for provider.execute, and it is the only action where the check exists.

Scope: the escape reaches only ops that devices may already approve (bounded ordinary writes/deletes, exact Calculator ops, tool-free Ollama is refused by its own branch). It gives no shell, code execution or provider full-tool authority, so it is not BLOCKER or HIGH. Because each post-expiry ask can be answered one action at a time, expiry does not stop ordinary remote approvals. That makes MEDIUM the right severity.

Note on the recommended fix: a deny in decide() for all oneTime answers on expired envelopes would also block workstation re-approval of expired Missions. Gating device answers in deviceRequestRefusal (for all actions) plus a deny in decide() for remote envelopes avoids that.

Not refuted. The finding reproduces, and the code matches the claimed lines.

Code paths verified:
- authorization.server.ts:346 `if (context.oneTime) return allow(...)` runs before the expiry check at :354 (`if (envelope.expiresAt <= now) return ask(...)`). The revoked check at :66 runs before the oneTime allowance, but there is no matching expiry check there. Agentic violations (:64) and the remote-execution ask (:339-342) do come before oneTime, so they are not affected.
- bus.server.ts:159 passes oneTime (from step.approvedOnce via manager.server.ts:1502/1575) into decide(), and :167 returns the allow unchanged.
- manager.server.ts respond() (~3422-3520) has no envelope expiry check for a plain Mission. The only device-side check is deviceRequestRefusal (:2008-2015), which tests expiry only inside the `request.action === "provider.execute"` branch. Other actions fall through to deviceApprovalRefusal and remoteExecutionRefusal, which do not check expiry.
- tickOnce (:879-907) checks only the runtime budget, not expiresAt, so the step still runs after the answer.
- Batches do check envelope expiry (batches.server.ts:194), so the oneTime path is inconsistent with batches and with the round-2 fix (12) intent.
- The existing test F01-R10 (remote-authority.test.ts:783-799) covers only provider.execute, so the gap is untested.

Probe (throwaway temp folder, removed afterwards; repo untouched):
- Mission with a filesystem.write step to an absolute path outside the approved write scope, approved by a device with start. The ask was pending.
- Control (envelope valid): device allow_once accepted, mission completed, file written.
- Variant: envelope.expiresAt set to now-1 after the ask was created. Device allow_once still accepted, mission completed, file "phone" written.

Impact is bounded. Code execution is still refused for devices by remoteExecutionRefusal and the desktopRequired check at deviceRequestRefusal:2011 (request.desktopRequired is first), so the reachable actions are non-code-execution operations (bounded file writes, Calculator ops, etc.). The defect is still a real authority-lifetime violation: a device extends an owner envelope past expiresAt, which the round-2 fix explicitly tried to prevent. The fix is incomplete, so MEDIUM is appropriate.

The out-of-scope write is accepted even with a valid envelope. That is one-time path approval by design, not part of this finding.

Coverage: no repo test was run and no repo file was changed. The probe folder was deleted. git status matches the starting snapshot.
